problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2

A water bottle with diameter of 6.5 cm, made of transparent material, is left lying sideways on the wooden floor on the terrace, which is fully exposed to the sun during the whole day.

1. Show that it can start a fire on the wood floor.

2. How far away from the line along which the bottle touches floor will the fire start?

3. What will be the angular position of the sun above the horizon?

State clearly all the assumptions and approximations you made.

The solar constant $s$ (the amount of solar radiation energy hitting the square meter surface) at the Earth surface is about 1 $kW/m^2$. Ignition temperature of wood is about 500 $^\circ$C.

The object at the temperature $T$ emits the energy $P = eA\sigma(T^4 - T_0^4)$ where $T_0$ is the surrounding temperature, $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma = 5.67\times10^{-8} W/m^2K$ and $A$ is the emitting surface. Assume emissivity of wood $e = 1$. Ignore the heat conductivity of wood.

You might find the following lens equations (which also approximately apply to the thick and cylindrical lenses) useful:

$$\frac{1}{d_i} + \frac{1}{d_0} = \frac{1}{f}$$

where $d_0$ is distance from lens to object, $d_i$ is the distance from lens to image, and $f$ is the focal length of the lens.

$$M = \frac{h_i}{h_0} = \frac{d_i}{d_0}$$

where $h_i$ and $h_0$ are the sizes of the image and object. $M$ is the magnification, which is the ratio of image size to object size.

The lens made of material with index of refraction $n$ with the surfaces of the radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ has a focal length $f$.

$$\tfrac{1}{f} = (n-1)(\tfrac{1}{R_1} - \tfrac{1}{R_2})$$

The h/d ratio for the sun is about 1/110. Index of refraction of water $n$=1.33

problems.title: Problem 3

Problem 3

A proton (mass $m_p = 938$ MeV/c$^2$) can be turned into a new particle called delta ($\Delta^+$, mass $m_\Delta = 1232$ MeV/c$^2$ when it absorbes a photon (denoted with $\gamma$, massless):

$$p^+ + \gamma \rightarrow \Delta^+ .$$

In such relativistic process, energy and momentum are necessarily conserved. The total relativistic energy of a particle depends on its momentum $p$ and mass $m$ through

$$E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2 ,$$

where $c$ is the speed of light. For a massless particle, this simplifies to

$$E = |p|c .$$

Consider an ultra-relativistic proton, whose speed is close to the speed of light and whose momentum is much larger than $m_pc$ absorbing a very low energy (long wavelength) photon in a head-on collision.

(a) Determine the total relativistic energy of the proton $E_p$ in terms of the (small) energy of the photon $E_\gamma$. Clearly state and justify all approximations made.

(b) If the absorbed photon has wavelength 1.063 mm, what must be the energy of the proton so that it is possible to produde a delta particle in such a head-on collision?

(c) If this photon were to collide with the proton at a different angle, would your answer to part (b) be larger or smaller?

[Constants from the data page of the paper: speed of light $c = 3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s; Planck's constant $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s; fundamental charge $e = 1.60\times10^{-19}$ C.]

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2

Birefringence is an optical phenomena where a birefringent crystal refracts light in two different directions, resulting in the separation of a single incident light beam into two polarized rays with different refractive indices ($n_o$ and $n_e$). These two rays are often called the ordinary ray (o-ray) and the extraordinary ray (e-ray). Each ray travels through the crystal at a different speed.

Part 1: Refraction from a birefringent crystal

When an electromagnetic wave propagates in a medium with a refractive index $n$, the change in oscillation phase after going through a distance $d$ can be expressed as follows.

$$\phi = \frac{2\pi n d}{\lambda}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cap-2024-2-2-fig1.png

a. Suppose we have a birefringent crystal with thickness $d$. If a beam of light with a wavelength of $\lambda$ propagates through the crystal, express the phase difference between the ordinary and extraordinary ray, $\phi$, in terms of $\lambda$, $n_e$, $n_o$, and $d$.

A beam of linearly polarized polychromatic light, whose electric field’s vector makes an angle $\theta = 45^\circ$ with the x-axis, falls normally on a crystal. The refractive index for the electric field component in the x-direction is $n_o = 2.647$, and the refractive index for the electric field component in the y-direction is $n_e = 2.693$.

b. Write down the conditions for the phase difference, $\phi$, that causes the transmitted light to have:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cap-2024-2-2-fig2.png

• i. Maximum intensity
• ii. Minimum intensity

c. It is known that the wavelengths for three primary colors are:

• $\lambda_{\text{red}} = 680\,\mathrm{nm}$
• $\lambda_{\text{green}} = 530\,\mathrm{nm}$
• $\lambda_{\text{blue}} = 470\,\mathrm{nm}$

Find the minimum thickness of the crystal, so that the transmitted light:

• i. Appears blue.
• ii. Appears yellow.

Part 2: Birefringent crystal and polarizers

A polarizer is an optical device that transmits electromagnetic waves with a particular orientation. For example, a linear polarizer at $\theta$ will selectively transmit the component of light oriented at $\theta$ as illustrated in the figure below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cap-2024-2-2-fig3.png

Now, our birefringent crystal is placed between two linear polarizers. The first (front) polarizer is aligned $\theta = 45^\circ$ clockwise with respect to the y-axis, while the second (rear) one is aligned $\theta = 45^\circ$ counter-clockwise with respect to the y-axis as shown in the figure below. An unpolarized light propagates normally to the first polarizer.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cap-2024-2-2-fig4.png

d. Write down the conditions for the phase difference, $\phi$, that causes the transmitted light to have:

• i. Maximum intensity
• ii. Minimum intensity

e. Find the minimum thickness of the crystal, so that the transmitted light:

• i. Appears blue.
• ii. Appears yellow.

problems.title: Problem 3. Physics of lightning
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Physics of lightning

Tall cumulonimbus clouds (thunder-clouds) host strong temperature gradients: lower layers contain water droplets, while upper layers form ice crystals or graupel. Collisions between them generate static charge within the cloud which also polarises the ground, establishing an electric field from the cloud to the ground, much like in a parallel-plate capacitor.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/cap-2026-2-3-fig1.png

When the downward electric field beneath the cloud reaches the breakdown value $E_{\mathrm{br}}$, electrons in air trigger an avalanche that forms a conducting channel. Lightning discharges the accumulated charge, after which the cycle repeats. Rain can carry some charge from the cloud to the ground. This leakage of charge slows down the charge buildup in the cloud, making the lightning less frequent or even stopping it altogether.

In this question we will study the effect of rainfall on rate of lightning.

Instructions: In parts (a)-(c) we require only symbolic answers and in (d) we require numerical answers.

(a) Rate of charge build up and breakdown. Let $Q$ be the total cloud charge over the footprint $A$. Show that when the breakdown field is reached, the value of the charge is

$$\boxed{Q_{\mathrm{br}} = \varepsilon_0\, A\, E_{\mathrm{br}}}$$

Before rainfall started, a lightning was seen roughly every $\Delta t_1 = 3\ min$. Using $Q_{\mathrm{br}}$, calculate $I_{\mathrm{int}}$, the average rate at which charge builds up internally in the cloud.

(b) Charge carried by rain. Treat a raindrop as a conducting sphere of radius $r_d$ carrying charge $q$, with surface tension $\gamma$ and permittivity $\varepsilon_0$. The charge a liquid droplet can carry is limited by its surface tension. As charge builds up, electrostatic repulsion pushes the surface outward while surface tension acts to hold it together. Using the interplay of these two forces, show that the largest stable charge—called the Rayleigh charge—is

$$\boxed{q_R = 8\pi\sqrt{\varepsilon_0\gamma\, r_d^3}}$$

Hint: You can calculate the electrostatic potential energy of a conducting shell by calculating the work done to add an infinitesimal charge $dq$ to a shell with charge $q$ and integrating. The surface energy is given by $\gamma\times$ surface area. If the total energy of the droplet decreases under an infinitesimal increase in its radius, it is energetically favorable for the droplet to expand or split. Alternatively, consider the balance between the outward electrostatic force on a small surface patch and the inward pull of surface tension along its boundary.

(c) Rain current to ground. Rate of rain $R$ is measured in the height of water that accumulates in a container per hour. If rain falls at rate $R$ (depth per unit time) over area $A$, the volume of water in the rain per unit time is $RA$. The charge appearing on a droplet takes a random value between zero and $q_R$. Assume on an average each drop carries only a fraction $\eta$ of the Rayleigh charge, $q_d = \eta q_R$. Show that the downward current to ground is

$$\boxed{I_{\mathrm{rain}} = 6RA\eta\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_0\gamma}{r_d^3}}}\,.$$

(d) Lightning during the rainfall

While charge builds up in the cloud at rate $I_{\mathrm{int}}$, charge carried out through the rain at the rate $I_{\mathrm{rain}}$. Based on $I_{\mathrm{rain}}$ calculated in the previous part, calculate symbolically the time interval $\Delta t_2$, that elapses before the next lightning strikes, once the rainfall begins.

Now use the data below to calculate $\Delta t_2$ numerically. Based on this number is it likely that one might see a lightning strike after rainfall begins?

Given constants (use orders of magnitude as needed). $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$, surface tension of water $\gamma = 0.072\,\mathrm{N/m}$, typical raindrop radius $r_d \sim 0.5\,\mathrm{mm}$, cloud footprint area $A \sim 25\,\mathrm{km^2}$, rainfall rate $R = 5\ mm/hr$. The air breakdown field is $E_{\mathrm{br}} \sim 2.5\times10^{6}\ V/m$. The fraction $\eta = 1/5$.
